speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Improvements in public infrastructure, sanitation and hygiene have drastically reduced the rates of then common serious infectious diseases, such as cholera and typhoid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Vaccination requirements, complemented by strong vaccination programmes, have resulted in high vaccination coverage against highly infectious diseases, such as measles and diphtheria.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Requirements for surveillance and reporting systems have also enabled the early detection of existing and new diseases, allowing for swift response to curtail disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Infectious pathogens and the environment in which we operate are continually changing, and we must regularly take stock of these changes and examine how we can better respond to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) recognises the following:  Firstly, Singapore is a densely-populated city-state, and a global travel and trade hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We remain vulnerable to the importation of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in 2003 is a stark reminder of how a new disease can wreak havoc on our healthcare system and socioeconomic fabric.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We have also experienced the influenza H1N1 pandemic in 2009 and, most recently, Zika in 2016.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Globally, ongoing outbreaks, which include Ebola in Africa and the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) in the Middle East, remind us of the need to be vigilant and to be prepared for the emergence of new diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We cannot just rely on the old traditional methodologies and must make provisions to allow for more effective and efficient ways – through information technology (IT), R&D or the use of technology – to prevent and control infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Lastly, while the Government takes the lead in safeguarding public health, infectious diseases can happen and spread anywhere – in homes, schools, workplaces and from overseas destinations – and we will need the help of the community to safeguard Singapore against these threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We received comments from members of the public, healthcare professionals, including infectious diseases specialists, academia and stakeholders from the telecommunications and transport sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Overall, respondents expressed support for the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There was also broad recognition that the amendments are intended to ensure that our legislative and regulatory measures to detect, prevent and control infectious diseases entering into and within Singapore, remain relevant and allow for the calibration of operations to manage the risk presented.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, let me introduce the amendments to enhance infectious disease surveillance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: With better understanding of certain infectious diseases and advancements in IT, there could be new ways of monitoring the health status of persons who may have infectious diseases of concern, for example, through remote or indirect means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This reduces the burden and inconvenience to the person being monitored and allows for a more scalable surveillance system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill clarifies the definition of "surveillance" in the Act to indicate that it may be periodic or continuous and explicitly provides a definition for medical examinations, which among others, could be conducted remotely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As it stands, both doctors and laboratories are required to notify my Ministry of the same set of infectious diseases when detected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: With the understanding that some infectious diseases come with distinctive clinical signs and symptoms which can be identified by doctors, while others can only be confirmed through laboratory testing, clauses 4 and 27 of the Bill clarify section 6, to allow for doctors, laboratories and any other prescribed groups of persons to report different prescribed sets of diseases to the Ministry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This will allow us to streamline notification requirements and reduce duplication.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: My Ministry undertakes public health surveillance where information and samples from healthcare facilities and laboratories are collected for testing and trend analysis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Strictly speaking, based on existing requirements, we must issue a new legal order each time we collect a sample, even though it may be an ongoing surveillance programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill amends section 7 to allow my Ministry to state, through a one-time order, the frequency and time period for the submission of samples or information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Next, allow me to introduce the amendments to prevent the introduction of infectious diseases into Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Under section 31, persons entering Singapore from specific areas must be required to be vaccinated against specified infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: There is currently no cure for Yellow Fever, but it can be easily prevented through vaccination which protects the individual from acquiring the disease.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To prevent the import of the disease into Singapore, we currently require travellers coming into Singapore from Yellow Fever endemic areas to show that they have been vaccinated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For these people, the Infectious Diseases Act provides for my Ministry to implement isolation or surveillance measures, or require them to undergo vaccination, to mitigate the risk of importation and possible spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Travellers who are non-citizens, may be refused entry into Singapore, if they do not comply with our measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While we can vaccinate and monitor small numbers of travellers, it would not be practicable to do so if the numbers increase to hundreds or even thousands, for example, if countries with high travel volume to Singapore are affected but fail to get their travellers vaccinated despite international advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In such a circumstance, the entry of large numbers of unvaccinated travellers poses both a health and public security threat to our community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: If necessary, we need to be able to protect ourselves against such threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Not all diseases are vaccine-preventable or serious enough for us to require all travellers from specific areas to show proof of vaccination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: At a more general level, it is important to have measures for us to identify unwell travellers who may be potential carriers or cases of infectious diseases, to facilitate early public health measures, such as treatment or isolation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As an example, travellers arriving from countries with an ongoing risk of MERS currently undergo temperature screening on arrival.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In a similar vein, Singapore should likewise be able to take steps to prevent the export of infectious diseases through unwell travellers to other countries, should we experience a serious outbreak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This was the case during the SARS outbreak, where travellers leaving Singapore had to undergo temperature screening.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These infectious disease control measures at the borders are currently provided for under Regulation 3 of the Infectious Diseases (Measures to Prevent or Control the Spread of Infectious Diseases) Regulations 2004.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These help reduce the risk of the introduction and spread of infectious diseases into the community in Singapore and the international spread of diseases from Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Lastly, I will introduce the amendments to strengthen infectious disease control within Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Regulation 4 of the Infectious Diseases (Measures to Prevent or Control the Spread of Infectious Diseases) Regulations 2004 provides for MOH to require workplaces and dormitories to conduct contact tracing and surveillance for specific diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This is to facilitate the identification and management of infected persons or contacts, to prevent disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The threat of infectious diseases is, however, not restricted to workplaces or dormitories alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: During the SARS outbreak, MOH put in place temperature monitoring of staff and students in schools, as a form of surveillance to identify and treat any infected persons, and prevent disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: More recently, in 2016, the detection of a cluster of tuberculosis cases in a block of flats in Ang Mo Kio was followed by the setup of onsite screening and contact tracing services to identify any other undiagnosed cases for follow-up treatment and monitoring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: While MOH had worked collaboratively with the relevant Government agencies, such as the Ministry of Education and the Housing Development Board to institute the respective measures, the experiences surfaced the potential need for legislative levers to require persons in charge of different types of premises to put in place surveillance or contact tracing measures to mitigate the spread of infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Following the detection of infectious diseases, a person may be restricted from his occupation under section 21, if the conduct of his occupation poses a risk of spread to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, food handlers tested positive for diseases that spread through food would be required to stop work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This stop-work requirement is a blanket one and does not facilitate allowing a worker to conduct other tasks, such as backend administration or cashiering that do not involve contact with food and, hence, would not spread the disease.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Clause 8 of the Bill calibrates section 21 to allow persons of a lower risk of transmission to perform specific occupational activities assessed to be acceptable from the disease transmission perspective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Likewise, clause 9 of the Bill amends section 21A to allow my Ministry to calibrate the restriction of movement placed on persons of lower risk of transmission, such as certain contacts of an infectious disease, to allow them some liberty to be at specified places, subject to conditions that would minimise the risk of disease exposure and transmission to others, instead of being disallowed in all public or common places outside of their homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, a low-risk contact may be allowed to go to his or her workplace via a specified mode of transport, such as a private car, for a certain period of time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I had spoken about the importance for my Ministry and other stakeholders to conduct surveillance and collect the necessary information to prevent disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In the event of an outbreak or potential disease spread, it is also of utmost importance that we have the means to push out critical information to the public such that they may take the necessary steps to protect their health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Besides information shared through mass media, there may be instances where targeted sharing to generate awareness among specific population groups is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, there would be value for persons travelling to or returning from a country affected by an outbreak to receive information concerning the disease and precautions to observe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: During the 2013 outbreak of H7N9 avian influenza in various parts of China, collaborative arrangements were made between my Ministry, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS), Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, Changi Airport Group and the relevant airlines, to distribute health advisory notices to travellers returning from affected areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This provision also provides the legal backing to operators required to disseminate information in different formats, including electronic ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Examples of operators include mobile operators, land, air and sea transport operators providing local and cross-border services, port and transport facility operators, persons who control or manage premises and event organisers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Section 21B also allows my Ministry to require operators to provide information of relevant persons to facilitate the dissemination of advisories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, if a case of measles or infectious tuberculosis is discovered on an airplane, we would need to obtain the airplane's passenger manifest, to provide passengers seated around the infectious person with information on the disease and mitigating actions to be taken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: When consulted, operators asked whether they would be in contravention of privacy laws, such as the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Even in our efforts to work with high-risk persons to prevent disease spread through necessary public health measures, a small minority may refuse to comply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: For example, an infectious person served an isolation order may abscond, totally disregarding the risk to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Section 56 currently allows such non-compliant persons to be arrested without warrant and to be punished, on conviction, with a penalty of a fine or jail term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: However, an arrest does not directly mitigate the immediate public health risk of disease transmission to others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It also makes explicit that persons under legal orders that restrict their movement in Singapore, would not be allowed to leave Singapore, unless otherwise permitted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: These provisions allow my Ministry to take steps to enforce the restrictions which are put in place on individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We are mindful that these powers should be exercised carefully and will put in place a framework for the assessment of cases, and safeguards, such as limiting the exercise of powers to specific situations, for example, where the immediate isolation of a highly infectious person is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, the disclosure of information for prevention of disease outbreak or spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To protect against the spread of infectious diseases, it is critical that entities responsible for carrying out disease prevention and control measures rapidly share information with one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Currently, section 57A of the Act requires, in certain circumstances, the Minister of Health's approval for the disclosure of information on infectious disease cases, carriers or contacts, from my Ministry to third parties for the purpose of preventing disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To provide for the direct sharing of such information among healthcare providers, as authorised by the Director of Medical Services, clause 22 inserts a new section 57B.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I give the example of infection by multi-drug resistant organisms, which can be transmitted through contact with a carrier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: A carrier of such organisms may seek care from different hospitals in different regional clusters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In this case, the sharing of information among hospitals is important, so that the necessary isolation measures can be taken to prevent the transmission of the disease to other patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Information shared may include the identifiers of the person and these should only be shared or used to the extent that allows the necessary measures to be taken to prevent disease spread.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We recognise that the use and disclosure of information should be conducted strictly on a need-to-know basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The healthcare services to which this new provision relates, and the conditions to be adhered to by the disclosing and receiving parties, will be specified.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: National public health research is an important tool to understand diseases and is necessary for the evaluation of current operations and identification of more efficient ways to manage or prevent outbreaks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Research outcomes include the development of preparedness plans and prevention and control policies, for the benefit of public health and to facilitate the optimal deployment of resources during an outbreak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We should not be doing research only when we are close to an emergency or already in one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: It is well-recognised that public health research needs to be conducted well in advance of any possible outbreak during peacetime, to ensure that Singapore's defences against any new or re-emerging infectious disease remain relevant and strong, so that we can effectively respond during an actual outbreak.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: We recognise the importance of protecting the confidentiality of persons and preventing potential misuse of data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: In using identifiable data, we will assess that it will benefit the greater public health interests of Singapore and there are no other reasonable alternative means to conduct the research.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Also, persons authorised to access identifiable data will be limited and must comply with conditions to ensure confidentiality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: As I come to the close of my speech, let me once again highlight my Ministry’s commitment to continue building on the good work which had been put into developing Singapore’s capabilities to prevent and control infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: Last year, Singapore was evaluated by the World Health Organization (WHO) on our capabilities in health security as stipulated through WHO's International Health Regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: My Ministry recognises that we must not and cannot afford to be complacent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The IDA is an important legal instrument that enables Singapore to prevent, protect against, control and respond to the spread of infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: This round of amendments to the Act was proposed following a detailed review of our existing levers and approaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: The proposed amendments are intended to achieve two key objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: First, to strengthen the Act based on the current infectious disease landscape and our operational experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: To sum up, the Infectious Diseases (Amendment) Bill is premised on the need to remain continually vigilant and maintain a high degree of preparedness against evolving infectious diseases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Health)
text: I ask for the support of all Members for this Bill.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although here in Singapore we remain rightly focused on the control of chronic diseases, such as diabetes, as they pose the greatest burden on our ageing population, we must never let our guard down on the threat that infectious diseases pose to a small, densely-populated country like ours.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The spectre of SARS, barely 15 years ago, remains fresh in many of our minds, and since then, many serious epidemics have occurred in many parts of the world, often spreading with frightening speed, both within the affected country and beyond its borders.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: WHO has published guidelines on how disease epidemics should be managed, but certainly, a key focus for any society would be, first, to prevent the spread of disease into the country, and, of course, later, following a disease outbreak, on how to contain its spread both within the country and beyond its borders.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments to this Bill are, therefore, timely as they seek to strengthen powers directed towards both epidemic prevention and containment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If one recalls the Ebola outbreaks in the not too distant past, we debated the measures that were available to safeguard Singapore by controlling the entry of travellers from the affected countries.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This had to be achieved via a rather circuitous route whereby travellers from countries with active and significant Ebola transmission had to obtain a temporary entry visa before travelling into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new sections 45A and 45B refer to monitoring activities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what if there is no accurate or practical means of screening travellers from hot zones?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the process of review and who are the entities that conduct such a review?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarifications on these points and support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Millions of tourists pass through our shores by air, land and sea.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think what we need to look into is how the frontline staff at the clinics and laboratory technicians are protected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What training is given to them to keep them abreast of preventive measures to be taken?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is the group that is vulnerable and they can be a source for spread of infectious diseases if they are not properly trained and protected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, we have seen from the outbreak of SARS how the frontline medical staff at the Government hospitals fell victim.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While we know the Government healthcare institutions are very vigilant and they conduct regular disease outbreak exercises to prepare their staff for such eventualities, unfortunately, I am not sure whether the same is true for non-Government hospitals and medical centres.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the MOH doing to ensure that their frontline staff also receive adequate protection?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How stringent are checks at privately-run clinical laboratories to ensure that the technicians and all those working there observe the necessary safety rules?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How often does MOH conduct audits of these laboratories where they handle blood, urine and other samples?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government make this mandatory for all hospital staff so that they do not become carriers because of the nature of their work in the hospital setting?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe, at present, it is not compulsory for all the staff, especially non-medical staff, like the receptionists, cleaners and so forth.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to ask the Minister what is the process in place if someone has visited a person or patient who is suffering from an infectious disease while overseas?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is this person required to declare upon embarking in Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there not a risk that this person could become a carrier though he or she may not have symptoms until after the gestation period?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there any public education that MOH will carry out to warn Singaporeans and others who travel abroad to visit a sick person?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe, in the setting of a public healthcare institution, staff are reminded if they return from, say, the Middle East, and have fever, they should report to the infectious disease control clinic for a check.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What about those who are not even in a healthcare setting?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For that matter, on the ground, what about the taxi that transports the person to the hospital?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am also concerned about how taxi drivers are protected against infectious diseases, especially against the avian flu.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to raise this point about the plastic trays used at airport checkpoints around the globe and touched by millions of passengers as they drop shoes, laptops, luggage and other items to clear X-ray scanners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In September this year, there were reports pointing out that studies have found that these trays carry a variety of germs, including the ones responsible for the common cold, according to researchers in Europe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Scientists from the University of Nottingham in England and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare swabbed frequently touched surfaces at Helsinki Airport in Finland during and after peak hours in the winter of 2016 and picked up traces of rhinovirus, the source of the common cold, and of the influenza A virus, reported the New York Times article.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is important for us to remember that the spread of infectious diseases is not to be taken lightly and there must not be any compromise in this regard.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is unfortunate that while modern medicine has eradicated many diseases, new ones are evolving and these are, at times, even more lethal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to reboot our vigilance and go back to basics and remind everyone, children to adults, such good habit as the importance of keeping our hands clean every time, all the time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The spread of infectious diseases cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, in public hospitals, measures to prevent infectious diseases are very stringent.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, doctors and nurses can enjoy free vaccinations against common infectious diseases.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do other staff from the hospital, such as the canteen staff and cleaners, enjoy the same benefits as well?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, for infectious diseases from overseas, MOH will make use of mobile phones and transport operators’ network to inform our people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that MOH can educate more Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: First of all, I would like to declare my interest as the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the recently amended Bill has been focused on strengthening contact tracing, surveillance, communication and the disclosure of information for infectious diseases.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is to my surprise that there is not much mention regarding the legalisation to curb the global and national issue of antibiotic resistance.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To provide some background information, antibiotic or antimicrobial resistance occurs when microbials or micro-organisms, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, change in ways that render the medications used to cure the infections they cause ineffective.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: When the micro-organisms become resistant to most antimicrobials, they are often referred to as "superbugs".

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This resistance occurs naturally but is facilitated by the inappropriate use of medicines, for example, using antibiotics for viral infections, such as cold or flu, sharing antibiotics or excessive inappropriate use of antibiotics in animals.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I shall henceforth refer to antimicrobial resistance as AMR.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: On 30 March 2017, a new Bill 1840 was brought before the United States (US) Congress to provide tax incentives to "reinvigorate" antibiotic research due to the grave nature of AMR.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The growing resistance of human infections to antimicrobial agents has emerged as one of the most pressing health problems in Singapore and the world.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the National Research Foundation (NRF) announced the launch of a new Antimicrobial Resistance Interdisciplinary Research Group in January 2018 in conjunction with the Singapore National Strategic Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, hopefully, to better understand how microbial resistance happens and to develop new antibiotics to curb these "superbugs".

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The economic burden will follow a similar trend as a result.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In the US alone, "AMR bacteria infect two million people every year at a healthcare cost of S$27 billion.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: So, at this rate, the world, including Singapore, will run out of antibiotics before long, and we might possibly go back to the era where even simple skin infections or urinary tract infections could kill us.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The severity of this threat should not be underestimated, and I urge that we deal with this issue critically and swiftly.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Tackling the AMR problem would require a multi-pronged and multifaceted approach.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge with relief that MOH has set up the National Strategic Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, engaging various Ministries and agencies, such as the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA), National Environment Agency, Public Utilities Board and so on, to evaluate various core strategies from public and healthcare professional education, surveillance and risk assessment, research, prevention and control of infection to the optimisation of antimicrobial use, and I applaud MOH for their tremendous effort in tackling this pressing threat.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: While a lot of surveillance and engagement work has been focused on hospitals since 2009, much more salient efforts have to be applied to get to the root of the problem.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This includes how we can further enhance our AMR surveillance to grasp the utilisation rate of diagnostic toolkits which can be used to differentiate viral and bacterial infections, as well as where and how much antibiotics are being sold, prescribed and dispensed in each hospital, general practitioner clinic, retail pharmacy and for animal use.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is then necessary to extract such detailed information and apply data analysis or audits to identify specific abusive users and establish a feedback mechanism for better accountability.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As such, I would like to propose measures that are imperative in resolving and lessening the impact of AMR in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to advocate an AMR taskforce to discuss and recommend strategies to ensure appropriate use of antibiotics in a community setting, such as the reviewing and streamlining of an antibiotics formulary available for perusal within the community and exploring prescribing-dispensing separations, where possible.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is also essential to urgently come up with clinical practice guidelines on the use of antibiotics, the appropriate course duration of use, as well as the conducting of audits on the appropriateness of antibiotics utilisation, especially for broad spectrum antibiotics like quinolones, in the community setting.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Educational programmes for healthcare providers in the United Kingdom (UK) have shown considerable effectiveness in reducing the prescription of antibiotics in primary care, and maybe similar programmes should be enacted in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This coverage should be extended nationwide and offered at a subsidised rate to our Pioneer Generation under the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS).

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Flu vaccinations should also be introduced into the national childhood immunisation programme to ensure that school children benefit from this and, at the same time, increasing the overall national take-up rate.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A 2017 systematic review published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health looked at studies that calculated the return on investment for public health interventions.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The researchers identified 52 studies that looked at interventions at local and national levels.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such a high return occurs because of all the disease and death prevented.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this review, a national public awareness programme should be incepted to educate the general public on the potential side effects and infections from the uninformed use of antibiotics.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens should be warned to refrain from asking for antibiotic prescriptions from their doctors.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Health Promotion Board (HPB) is already working on this, but more aggressive and intense public education campaigns must be carried out to raise urgent attention.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Other potentially deadly side effects due to drug allergies include anaphylaxis, a life-threatening allergic reaction, or fatal skin reactions like the Stevens Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), fungal infections which lead to severe itching from vaginal yeast infections or burning mouth sores from oral thrush, and antibiotics-associated diarrhoea.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There is a compelling need to empower patients to speak up and discuss risks versus benefits of imbibing antibiotics with their doctors to help them take ownership of their own health.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Emphasis on the importance of hand hygiene and infection preventive measures in the community should not be understated.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, the importance of flu vaccination and the fact that getting vaccinated protects loved ones around you, such as those more vulnerable to serious flu illnesses like babies and young children, as well as older people and people with certain chronic health conditions.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is possible through the vaccine herd effect or herd immunity, which makes a disease hard to spread because there are very few people who are susceptible.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To facilitate these actions, the use of rapid diagnostic health devices should be promoted and distributed widely at a highly subsidised rate.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will make it more cost-effective to use these devices compared to paying for a course of antibiotics.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: AMR is a major worldwide complication that has persisted and will continue to persist.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is something that we simply cannot afford to disregard in the slightest if we are not to invite disastrous consequences.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It requires the synergistic coordination and collaboration of everyone in Singapore to combat and safeguard against.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The cooperation of citizens, operators, healthcare professionals, diagnostic and pharmaceutical industries, educators, researchers, various Government Ministries and policymakers should be sought out in order to fend off this dire situation.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Globally, many countries struggle with this deplorable predicament.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I firmly believe that Singapore, being a country of first-world infrastructure and data management, armed with capabilities of a Smart nation, can and should employ data analytics and her pool of highly educated citizens to weather this storm.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am certain that we can proclaim to the world that it is, indeed, possible to come out on top and rein in AMR.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, indeed, it is timely to have it updated and reviewed, looking also at the current state of affairs of the world with the spectrum of new, emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In doing this, Singapore must continue to stand guided by global bodies, such as WHO and the Communicable Diseases Centre (CDC).

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the institution level, all our restructured hospitals have got an action plan and also a response plan.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do we also wait for MOH, WHO and CDC advisories?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the coordination like on a bigger scale at the global or even regional levels?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Is there a direct chain of communications and correspondence for Singapore that has been established?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do the environmental and health organisations of both countries have a modus operandi in place?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Third, temperature scanners these days are not commonly seen at our borders as compared to the period during the SARS outbreak.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Does this mean that we rely entirely on people and travellers declaring that they are ill at our points of entry?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister please just comment on this as well?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, in dealing with infectious diseases and notification, there is a need to report particulars and details.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, disclosures and consent become compulsory and are given significant weightage.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In this day and age of the PDPA and handling information and particulars with utmost confidentiality, we will definitely have to strike a balance between this and upholding public health policies and principles.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, would MOH be embarking on more public awareness and education programmes to help the frontline medical personnel when we are having issues with outbreaks and handling infectious diseases, including antibiotic resistance as well?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I notice that HPB has already started an educational campaign on that matter.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is our framework with CAAS and also other airlines?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How fast can contact tracing and ringfencing be done?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And this is critical because our borders are really very open these days.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With these clarifications, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned by the hon Members of Parliament who spoke before me, in particular, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Singapore is an international travel hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These travellers come from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Greater travel connectivity and movement of people come with the attendant risk of the spread of diseases, something that the hon Senior Minister of State Dr Lam Pin Min highlighted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These proposed amendments to the IDA allow the Government to enhance infectious disease surveillance and equip us to better prevent the spread of infectious diseases both within Singapore and from outside Singapore into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead of a blanket ban against carrying on any occupation, trade or business, which is presently the case, the amendments allow the authorities to make an assessment of the extent of risk in the circumstances, and make appropriate orders as necessary to prevent the transmission of infectious diseases, which may not need to be a complete cessation of trade or business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the learned Senior Minister of State mentioned food handlers as an example.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This calibrated approach will be less disruptive to businesses and traders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The amendments, however, do not provide direct assistance to a person who has been ordered by the Director to cease business to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To illustrate, if a person is a carrier of an infectious disease, such as dengue or measles, is afflicted and he is asked to be quarantined, for certain occupations, such as self-employed persons like taxi drivers, they may still have to honour their contractual arrangements with their counterparties, for example, the taxi companies, for the period they should be quarantined, so that they will not infect their passengers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is commonly provided in agreements between taxi companies and their drivers that they have to pay rent for the hire of the taxi if they have a medical certificate (MC) for longer than a defined period, for example, seven days.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This creates a potential conundrum for the self-employed person who may be caught between a rock and a hard place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If they abide by the Director's orders, they may be exposed to liability vis-a-vis the counterparties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I met a gentleman at a funeral wake of his relative.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He related to me that he was given 14 days' MC for his infectious disease.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, he was required to pay rent after an initial seven-day period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was unable to secure cover because of the suddenness of the situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He had no choice but to pay rent even though he was quarantined at home on his doctor's orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, section 20 of the UK Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984, provides for local authorities to, by notice in writing, request any person to discontinue work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And, in such instances, the local authorities may have to compensate the person if he has suffered any loss in complying with such a request.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 20 of the UK Act has since been repealed and replaced with regulation 8 of the UK Health Protection (Local Authority Powers) Regulations 2010 which continues to enable the local authorities to offer compensation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from a written request in writing to stop work, section 45H of the Public Health (Control of Diseases) Act also allows for local authorities to apply to a Justice of the Peace for an order to impose restrictions or requirements to protect human health.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The order made may order the payment of compensation or expenses in connection with the taking of measures pursuant to the order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point is that the UK provisions contemplate the authorities giving compensation where a worker's work or trade has been affected by a measure taken in protection of public health, such a stop-work order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Singapore, we do not have that, which means that the risks may lie entirely with the trader or worker concerned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, section 6 of the Act is proposed to be amended to require certain persons who are aware or suspects that another person is suffering from, or is a carrier of, a prescribed infectious disease, to notify the Director of Medical Services of those facts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The section previously made reference to "infectious disease", which is specified in the First Schedule of the Act, instead of "prescribed infectious disease".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The amendments also provide that what amounts to "prescribed infectious disease" will be set out in Regulations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the Act already spells out what amounts to infectious disease in the First Schedule, and also separately spells out what is dangerous infectious disease in the Second Schedule, may I please ask what will be covered under the new defined term of "prescribed infectious disease"?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How will the list of prescribed infectious disease be drawn up?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Will there be any interplay between the infectious diseases set out in the First Schedule and the list of prescribed infectious diseases?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in that regard, we should never forget the heroes, such as Nurse Hamidah Ismail and Dr Alex Chao, who lost their lives in helping Singaporeans during the SARS incident, and they always would deserve our eternal debt of gratitude.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most effective responses to infectious diseases are steps that are taken pre-emptively to curb the risk of any emerging threats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill provides the stakeholders with the necessary powers to respond ahead of time of any outbreaks, and quickly, should an outbreak actually occur.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I also believe that all powers should be accompanied by checks and balances and I would like to seek some clarifications on the broad powers the Bill provides.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 21(1), the Director may give directions to any individual to cease or to change how they carry out any occupation, trade or business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I note that section 21(2)(a) states that the Director will specify the "period of time" that the individual will have to cease their occupation, trade or business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the decision be made by just one person or a committee?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, section 17A, which allows the Minister to declare a public health emergency and designate restricted zones, is subject to a 14-day time limit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no similar time limit for the Director’s powers under section 21(1).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide the assurance that reasonable periods, subject to regular reviews, will be preferred over long bans?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, under section 57B(1), a healthcare provider may disclose information identifying a person as an individual affected or suspected to be affected by an infectious disease.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The healthcare provider must be authorised by the Director to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 57B(3) the specified recipient of information may further disclose that information to another person providing a prescribed healthcare service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The disclosure is only to the extent necessary to prevent the spread or outbreak of the infectious disease.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on whether the extent necessary is at the sole judgement of the specified recipient, and whether the Director's authorisation or affected person’s consent would be required?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 57B(6) defines "healthcare provider" and "specified recipient" as any person that provides a prescribed healthcare service which will be prescribed in subsequent regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share in advance the scope of healthcare services that may be prescribed and whether a "healthcare provider" would be limited to medical practitioners registered under the Medical Registration Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to section 57B, section 59A(5A) also allows individually-identifiable information to be disclosed for the purpose of national public health research.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are no express provisions for both section 57B and section 59A on safeguards that may be imposed on the recipient of such information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Rather, section 57B(2) and section 59A(5)(c) allow the Director to impose conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I assume that these conditions will require the recipient of the information to take steps to prevent further disclosure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the subsidiary legislation or guidelines further elaborate on the safeguards that recipients must put in place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to commend MOH on the six-week public consultation that was conducted in mid-2018 on the proposed amendments to the IDA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, unlike the draft Healthcare Services Bill, there was no direct response from the Ministry to the public consultation feedback.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, we would have to, first, offer this group vaccination, surveillance or isolation before turning them away if they refuse.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the event of a sudden influx of visitors from places with ongoing outbreaks, the new legislative framework would help to reduce the risk of exposure to our people and avert the problem of capacity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I fully agree with the Ministry’s recommendation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are the vaccination certificates presented when they arrive in Singapore or at the point of embarkation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think it is a safer arrangement for us to have pre-emptive arrangements with foreign ports to require travellers present proof before they depart for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would enable us to screen out potential disease carriers and prevent their contact with other travellers coming here and our immigration staff.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is much better than allowing them to make the journey here and, subsequently, turning them away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My second question is that if the vaccination certificates were presented before they board the transport vehicles, do our officers check and verify these documents again when they arrive in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Travel, particularly air travel, continues to grow rapidly around the world.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This means that a potentially dangerous pathogen could spread globally within days.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is of paramount importance that we manage our exposure risks with best practices and technologies available.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet, the precautionary screening measures we have at our airports, ferry terminals and other checkpoints seem minimal and easy to get around.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, medication can lower body temperatures and thus render infrared cameras less effective.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another major challenge is that carriers may not be aware of their illnesses nor have symptoms.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the tools being developed will detect respiratory diseases using ion mobility spectrometry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we have any such local research initiatives?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How much control will the Ministry have over the channels and platforms used, such as the printed materials, television, radio, the Internet and social media?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be some form of monitoring to ensure the integrity and quality of the health advisory delivery.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The information should be provided in our four official languages and even some foreign languages, wherever possible.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Another important amendment is to empower our health officials to use other means, in addition to arrest, to restrict the movement of high-risk persons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of them may have already been infected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Others may have been exposed to infected persons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For some non-compliant individuals and their families, such restraints on their movements, especially when they have not shown syndromes, can be very frustrating, even unpleasant, and emotions can run high.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To pre-empt and counter such reactions, I would like to suggest that we include such scenarios as part of our emergency preparedness and public education.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regular public advisories to inform and educate all residents of the necessary measures for such crises will help prepare them mentally.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: People need time to adjust and accept difficult measures psychologically.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Another important amendment is to empower our health officers to use other means, in addition to arrest, to restrict the movement of high-risk persons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these may have come down with the infections, others may have been exposed to infected persons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For some non-compliant individuals and their families, such restraints on their movements, especially when they have not shown symptoms, can be very frustrating.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The entire experience is expectedly inconvenient, even unpleasant, and emotions can run high.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To pre-empt and counter such reactions, I would like to suggest that we include such scenarios as part of our emergency preparedness and public education.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regular public advisories to inform and educate all residents of the necessary measures for such crises will help prepare them mentally.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: People need time to adjust and accept difficult measures psychologically.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All these preparedness measures will better equip Singapore for health crises and keep us safe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore is an open and connected country, and we receive well over 17 million visitors a year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While our openness has benefited the economy, a tradeoff that we accept is that it puts us at an increased risk of suffering from infectious diseases that may be carried over from other countries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Members of this House and, indeed. many Singaporeans, would remember the SARS outbreak in 2003, and how we narrowly escaped MERS in 2012.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The review of the IDA is thus timely, but I have some clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I fully agree that this is necessary and critical in the event of an infectious disease outbreak, there needs to be a safeguard in place to ensure that this power does not go unchecked.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Minister clarify if there are, or would be, any safeguards in place, or if there is a maximum number of consecutive days that a person can be subjected to medical surveillance?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is similarly a directive that would affect business continuity as well as workers’ livelihood.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such orders can be reviewed and a new order could be reissued if the situation still warrants it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With freelancers and workers in the gig economy not covered by hospitalisation leave offered by employers, there is a large possibility of a loss of income following such directives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To better aid the appointed health officers, some of whom would have to perform contact tracing, I would like to suggest establishing a pool of volunteer Health Officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Organisations can be large and have multiple worksites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It can, therefore, be challenging and time consuming for a Health Officer to perform contact tracing without some forthcoming help.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, the number of Health Officers that we have is limited.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would, therefore, like the Ministry to consider establishing a volunteer Health Officer scheme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The desired outcome is for every large organisation to have an appointed volunteer Health Officer, who can aid a Health Officer in contact tracing as well as help to disseminate health advisories in the event of a crisis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This pool of volunteer Health Officers should be provided with adequate training to ensure they have the required skills to perform proper contact tracing and assist our Health Officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that we put in place rigorous safeguards for the use and disclosure of such data to protect the privacy and confidentiality of individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What safeguards will the Ministry put in place, and how will the Ministry ensure that third-party researchers adhere to these rules?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will conclude by saying that, due to the nature of our economy, Singapore will always be at risk of infectious diseases carried from other countries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments proposed are useful and timely in helping to enhance surveillance and prevent the introduction and spread of infectious diseases within our shores.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we need to ensure that while we fight against the spread of infectious diseases, we do not inevitably cause irreversible disruptions to everyday life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Infectious pathogens and the environment in which we operate can and will change.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry has put in place safeguards to ensure that use of the powers under the Act is commensurate with the public health concerns to be addressed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Members have sought clarifications on the proposed amendments and some of our operational measures.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Everyone has a part to play in preventing and controlling infectious diseases, and it is important to provide people with information to allow them to do so.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry has initiatives to reach out to both the general population and specific groups.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, the HPB's "FIGHT the Spread of Infectious Diseases" campaign encourages the public to practise good hygiene measures, such as frequent hand washing and keeping up to date with immunisations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For childcare centres, we have developed the Infection Control Guidelines for Schools and Child Care Centres on recommended practices to reduce disease spread among staff and students.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Sometimes, during an outbreak, there is a need to inform specific groups of persons about how to protect themselves, the symptoms to look out for and when to seek medical help, in an effective and targeted manner.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, during the 2013 Avian influenza outbreak in parts of China, my Ministry worked with the Changi Airport Group and airlines with flights arriving from affected areas, to disseminate health advisory notices to their passengers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Ms Joan Pereira indicated, beyond cooperative arrangements, situations may arise where we would need to rapidly engage operators to effectively reach out to target populations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, an airline is in a good position to distribute information, in the appropriate languages, to its passengers travelling to, or returning from, an outbreak area.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Likewise, a mobile phone service operator may be able to quickly send information to its subscribers travelling in an affected country.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we need to push out information to persons in a convenient way, for example, without requiring them to take special actions, such as opting into a service or downloading an app.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry will formulate the content and messaging and coordinate with operators on the most appropriate form of dissemination.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Ms Joan Pereira commented on measures at the borders to prevent the introduction of infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will first address the comments on declaration of one's health status and travel history after visiting a high-risk area.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While my Ministry has taken measures to raise awareness and seek cooperation, we also recognise that awareness levels may differ and not everyone may exercise personal responsibility in measures, such as self-declaration.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We must have the powers and capabilities to detect infectious diseases at our borders when needed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, it is not practical nor feasible to screen everyone for all diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Infectious diseases vary in severity and how easily they spread.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To efficiently allocate resources and avoid unnecessary burden to travellers, my Ministry conducts risk assessments, taking into account infectious disease developments around the world and international practices, prior to adopting technology and implementing surveillance measures.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, temperature screening at the airport is currently limited to flights from countries in the Middle East at risk of MERS transmission.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Screening is done at the aerobridge to target at-risks persons and minimise inconvenience to others.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It allows my Ministry to mitigate the risks presented by persons who arrive in Singapore without having undergone such vaccinations or prophylaxis.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Refusing entry to all travellers from a country with an outbreak of a specific disease will need to be in line with our laws and international obligations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu also said that there may not be established surveillance measures for certain diseases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Border surveillance does not pick up persons with infectious diseases during the incubation period.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: That is why we advise persons who have travelled to high-risk areas to seek medical attention should they develop symptoms.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our healthcare professionals in primary care clinics and emergency departments are very much on the frontline and need to be vigilant in picking up imported cases.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef sought clarification on our coordination structures during outbreaks, both domestically and internationally.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry taps on the International Health Regulations' National Focal Point network to communicate with WHO and other countries.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All countries are required to have a National Focal Point accessible at all times to share information.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry has also established links with WHO, our counterpart agencies and international experts, to obtain and share information early.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is especially important in time-sensitive situations where we need to act while pending, for example, WHO's advice.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Locally, my Ministry maintains a close working relationship with other Ministries, Government agencies and stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Homefront Crisis Management System allows us to harness the expertise across agencies and coordinate preparedness and responses to crises, including infectious disease threats.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To ensure that preparedness plans are continually strengthened, regular joint exercises and reviews are conducted.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry has channels of communication with our land, air and sea checkpoints through the Immigration and Checkpoints, Civil Aviation and Maritime and Port authorities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the event of a severely ill passenger suspected of having an infectious disease, there are arrangements in place between these authorities and my Ministry that cover the medical assessment, conveyance and management of the ill passenger, as well as the handling of other passengers and the vessel itself.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Airlines are guided by international standards provided by the International Civil Aviation Organization, the International Air Transport Association and WHO on routine cleaning and standard disinfection procedures for aircrafts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These procedures apply while investigations are underway for a suspected case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Upon confirmation of a serious disease which may require additional disinfection procedures, the IDA provides the powers for my Ministry and the National Environment Agency to require them to be carried out.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Likewise, these powers are applicable to other types of vehicles.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry is working with CAAS and the airline association to examine how we can better educate travellers from affected countries on the need for Yellow Fever vaccination.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Airlines have the burden of bringing travellers who are denied entry back to the country of embarkation, so they have a strong incentive to remind and verify that travellers have been vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On this note, I want to echo what Mr Murali Pillai has said in recognising all the hard work provided by our healthcare professionals, especially during times of crisis.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry takes the protection of our healthcare staff very seriously.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have operational requirements and guidelines to prevent and control disease spread in the healthcare setting.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry provides advice and guidelines to hospitals, clinics, nursing homes and registered healthcare professionals, such as recommendations on vaccinations, information on specific diseases, such as MERS, workflows on assessing a patient's travel history, and clinical management.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Ms Irene Quay had mentioned, the interaction of the human, environment and animal sectors, and AMR is very complex.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To further build our capability to tackle AMR, my Ministry had set up the AMR Coordinating Office last year within the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This office, together with our other capabilities, including the National Public Health Laboratory, and infectious disease research, plays a key role in coordinating with stakeholders and shaping initiatives in surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, education and infection control.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In preventing and controlling outbreaks, there is often a need to use the information of cases and contacts of infectious diseases for interventions, such as contact tracing, surveillance or response by healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: My Ministry has in place operational processes to ensure the lawful use or disclosure of personal information for the purposes of the Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As an added safeguard, the healthcare provider disclosing the information and the specified person receiving the information under the new section 57B must comply with conditions imposed by the Director of Medical Services in authorising such disclosure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
